items.explanation: In Sonnet 108, the final sonnet of Sir Philip Sidney's Astrophil and Stella (1591), Astrophil remains trapped in an unresolved paradox of despair and devotion, concluding 'That in my woes for thee thou art my joy, / And in my joys for thee my only annoy' without achieving resolution.

items.title: Q3 · Sept 2013 Reconduct (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: Who among the following English writers opposed the Licensing Act of 1643 ?

structured.lead:
Who among the following English writers opposed the Licensing Act of
1643 ?
structured.options_hint: John Milton Thomas Browne Andrew Marvell

items.explanation: John Milton fiercely opposed Parliament's Licensing Order of June 1643 in his landmark prose polemic Areopagitica (1644). Addressed to the English Parliament, it eloquently defended freedom of the press and argued against pre-publication censorship.

items.title: Q4 · Sept 2013 Reconduct (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Joseph Addison
items.stem: Who claimed : "I have not published a single paper that is not written in a spirit of benevolence and with a love of mankind" ?

structured.lead:
Who claimed : "I have not published
a single paper that is not written in a spirit of benevolence and with a love of mankind" ?
structured.options_hint: Pope Dryden Swift Addison

items.explanation: Joseph Addison made this remark regarding his periodical essays in The Tatler and The Spectator (1711–12), which sought to 'enliven morality with wit, and to temper wit with morality' in a spirit of benevolence rather than harsh personal satire.

items.title: Q5 · Sept 2013 Reconduct (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: A protagonist writes a letter of confession, but it gets lost under the carpet only to be found on the wedding day. Who is the protagonist ?

structured.lead: A protagonist writes a letter of confession, but it gets lost under the carpet only to be found on the wedding day. Who is the protagonist ?
structured.options_hint: Bathsheba Lucetta Sue Tess

items.explanation: In Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), Tess Durbeyfield writes a four-page letter confessing her past with Alec d'Urberville and slips it under Angel Clare's door before their wedding. It slides beneath the carpet unseen, and Tess discovers it unread on her wedding morning.

items.title: Q6 · Sept 2013 Reconduct (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In an age of pressurized happiness, we sometimes grow insensitive to subtle joys. The italicised words are an example of

structured.lead: In an age of pressurized happiness, we sometimes grow insensitive to subtle joys. The italicised words are an example of
structured.options_hint: a transferred epithet a simile a metapho

items.explanation: In the phrase 'pressurized happiness,' the adjective 'pressurized' is grammatically attached to the abstract noun 'happiness,' even though it is actually the people living in the modern age who feel pressurized. Shifting an adjective from a person to an associated noun is a transferred epithet (hypallage).

structured.options_hint: The abolition of the Lord Chamberlain's

options: The abolition of the Lord Chamberlain's office in 1968
The illegal performance of works by Howard Brenton and Edward Bond
The collapse of liberal humanist consensus in the late 1960s
A combined appeal to the Queen by a group of London dramatists
items.explanation: The Theatres Act 1968 abolished the Lord Chamberlain's centuries-old power of stage censorship in Britain (which had been enforced since the Licensing Act of 1737), allowing British theatre companies to commission and perform politically, socially, and sexually controversial plays freely.

structured.lead: "We will do it, I tell you; we will do it." The repetition of a phrase is
structured.options_hint: Antiphrasis Diacope Aposiopesis Enumerat

items.explanation: In classical rhetoric, 'diacope' (from the Greek for 'cutting in two') is the repetition of a word or phrase broken up by one or more intervening words for emphasis—here, repeating 'we will do it' with 'I tell you' inserted between.

items.stem: Which one of the following characters in Shakespeare's Tempest is associated with the Earth ?

structured.lead: Which one of the following characters in Shakespeare's Tempest is associated with the Earth ?
structured.options_hint: Ferdinand Ariel Caliban Prospero

items.explanation: In William Shakespeare's The Tempest (1611), Prospero explicitly addresses his enslaved servant Caliban as 'Thou earth, thou!' (Act I, Scene 2), associating Caliban's heavy, physical, and instinctual nature with the element of earth, in contrast to the spirit Ariel, who embodies air and fire.

items.title: Q17 · Sept 2013 Reconduct (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: In the Advancement of Learning Bacon attempted a preliminary survey of the entire field of learning, by analyzing the principal obstacles to its advancement. Identify from among the following choices the one that he did not mention as an obstacle

structured.lead:
In the Advancement of Learning
Bacon attempted a preliminary survey of the entire field of learning, by analyzing the principal obstacles to its advancement. Identify from among the following choices the one that he did not mention as an obstacle
structured.options_hint: Rhetoric Medieval scholasticism Inductiv

items.explanation: In The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon identified three main 'distempers' or obstacles to learning: 'delicate learning' (excessive rhetoric), 'contentious learning' (medieval scholasticism), and 'fantastical learning' (pseudo-sciences). Rather than an obstacle, the inductive empirical method was Bacon's championed path forward.

structured.options_hint: Tom Bertram John Thorpe James Morland He

items.explanation: In Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey (1817), James Morland and John Thorpe are fellow students at Oxford University, and in Mansfield Park (1814), Tom Bertram also attends Oxford. By contrast, Henry Tilney in Northanger Abbey is already an ordained clergyman and is not sent to the university during the narrative.

items.explanation: In Hard Times (1854), Charles Dickens caricatures Jeremy Bentham's and James Mill's utilitarian philosophy through schoolmaster and MP Thomas Gradgrind, a 'man of realities' and 'calculations' who opens the novel demanding 'Nothing but Facts!' and suppresses imagination in his children.

structured.lead: Which one of the following playwrights will not be covered under the category / term 'Theatre of the Absurd' ?
structured.options_hint: Jean Genet Jean Giraudoux Samuel Beckett

items.explanation: In his landmark study The Theatre of the Absurd (1961), Martin Esslin grouped Samuel Beckett, Eugène Ionesco, and Jean Genet as major Absurdist dramatists. Jean Giraudoux (1882–1944), author of Tiger at the Gates and The Madwoman of Chaillot, belonged to an earlier French tradition of philosophical and mythic drama.

items.explanation: Derived from the Greek for 'name-making,' onomatopoeia is a figure of speech in which a word's pronunciation imitates or suggests the natural sound it describes, such as 'buzz,' 'hiss,' 'murmur,' or 'clang.'

options: Britain's pre-eminence as a global power will depend on mastery of foreign languages
Abandon the introspection of the Romantics and turn to the higher moral purpose found in Goethe

items.explanation: In Book II, Chapter 9 ('The Everlasting Yea') of Sartor Resartus (1833–34), Thomas Carlyle's persona Diogenes Teufelsdröckh exhorts readers to 'Close thy Byron; open thy Goethe,' urging Victorians to abandon self-absorbed Romantic introspection and despair in favour of dutiful moral action.

structured.options_hint: writerly text aesthetic text readerly te

items.explanation: In S/Z (1970), Roland Barthes distinguishes between the 'readerly' (lisible) text, which conceals its artifice to offer passive consumption of a fixed meaning, and the 'writerly' (scriptible) text, which draws attention to its own structure and invites the reader to actively co-produce meaning.

items.explanation: Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock is a mock-heroic poem written in heroic couplets and published in two versions of two cantos (1712) and five cantos (1714) to reconcile two Catholic families. Pope's tribute to Queen Anne and the Peace of Utrecht is his poem Windsor-Forest (1713).

items.explanation: John Dryden's allegorical verse satire Absalom and Achitophel (1681) directly captures the Restoration political and religious turmoil of the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis (1679–81), when the Earl of Shaftesbury (Achitophel) sought to exclude the Catholic Duke of York from the throne.

items.explanation: In his verse epistle Ars Poetica (c. 19 BC), the Roman poet Horace formulated the influential critical maxim utile dulci ('profit combined with delight'), declaring that the ideal poet wins every vote by blending moral instruction with aesthetic pleasure.

items.explanation: From 1816 until his death in 1834, Samuel Taylor Coleridge lived at the home of Dr. James Gillman in Highgate, north of London, where young writers, philosophers, and admirers attended his famous Thursday evening conversations, earning him the title 'The Sage of Highgate.'
